title: 2026 Predictions for UX
intro: His ten predictions for 2026, published in the 2025 year-in-review — “the tradition of me making ill-thought-out predictions”. He scores his 2025 set at about 8.5/10.

learn.title: What senior researchers get hired for
learn.text:
**Judgment, not method coverage.** The strongest researchers will be hired less for what methods they can run and more for **what they can stop**: saying no, slowing teams down, calling out weak logic.

**Fixing inputs, not running studies.** The best will be pulled upstream to define questions, success criteria and evidence standards before any research happens — less visible work, much more valuable.

**ROI becomes a must-have.** Not inherently a researcher's job, but squarely within our strengths.

try.q: What does Calabro predict senior researchers will be valued for?
options: The size of the research team they manage
try.explain: Saying no, slowing teams down and calling out weak logic become core expectations.

right.label: Valued in 2026
items: Questions and evidence standards set upstream
Impact shown in cost, risk or revenue

learn.title: The split in UX maturity
learn.text:
Companies will fall into two camps, and the gap will become impossible to ignore.

**System-driven orgs** can explain decisions, trade-offs and ROI.
**Vibes-driven orgs** keep shipping confident-looking products that underperform once they meet real market conditions.

Related: **ResearchOps will matter more than ever** — one great researcher can't fix a broken system. Teams that improve will invest in templates, decision logs, evidence standards and repeatable workflows. The ones that don't will keep burning out their strongest people.

try.q: What will separate the two camps of UX maturity?
options: Whether they can explain decisions, trade-offs and ROI
How much they spend on research
How quickly they ship new features
try.explain: One group can explain; the other ships confident-looking products that underperform.

learn.title: Four more
learn.text:
**Synthetic users quietly fall out of favour** — what looks like insight is often automated bias confirmation. By late 2026, AI proxy users start to feel embarrassing in serious research orgs.

**Heuristic reviews regain credibility as a senior skill** — expert evaluation grounded in task flow and real context, as teams tire of expensive studies answering obvious questions.

**“Delight” stays misunderstood** — more bad animation, less proper labelling, more friction.

**Accessibility stops being a checklist** — discussed as failure modes, legal exposure and task breakdowns instead.

**Reporting gets shorter and sharper** — concise readouts, shared docs and short clips, with real recommendations.

try.q: Why does he expect heuristic reviews to regain credibility?
options: Teams tire of expensive studies answering obvious questions
Automated tools now run them reliably
They are cheaper than recruiting participants
Regulators have started requiring expert review
try.explain: Expert-driven evaluation grounded in task flow and real-world context.
